knapsack: Why scale profits rather than weights?

A pseudo-polynomial DP already solves the exact problem; its number of states depends on a numerical value. We will change the objective units, keep the original weights for feasibility, and charge the rounding error to a computable lower bound on OPT.
In scheduling the same idea compresses job sizes, but feasibility now needs a restoration argument.
scheduling-scheme: Where does the rounding error go?

A guessed makespan separates long jobs from short jobs. Rounded long-job configurations make the search finite; restoring original lengths and inserting short jobs are different steps and require different bounds.
Bin packing uses a related compression, but the best guarantee includes an additive term.
bin-scheme: Why an additive bin cannot be ignored

Large items force a combinatorial packing problem; small items can be inserted afterward. Linear grouping reduces the number of large types while isolating a discarded group whose cost must remain visible.
Next, randomness will replace type compression as the mechanism for controlling a large search space.
sat-random: From a random assignment to a deterministic algorithm

Count a clause as an indicator and compute its satisfaction probability before summing. Independence belongs inside each clause calculation; linearity of expectation does not require different clauses to be independent.
The next lecture compares the random assignment with an LP and asks how two imperfect guarantees can complement each other.
sat-lp: A relaxation is a bound, not yet an assignment

The LP spreads truth mass across variables. We will compare clause satisfaction after rounding with the fractional clause value, then combine guarantees without switching the maximization-ratio convention.
The applications that follow preserve a different constraint in each problem; the rounding analysis must change with it.
pcst: Turn fractional inclusion into an actual tree
Separate connection cost from omitted-vertex penalties. Thresholding chooses which terminals to connect, and each part of the objective needs its own comparison with the fractional solution.
Facility location also rounds inclusion decisions, but nearby clients need coordinated openings.
facility: Why independent openings leave a gap

A fractional assignment can spread one client across many facilities. Clustering first creates representatives and disjoint opening decisions; the distance analysis must account for reassignment to a representative.
Scheduling replaces spatial distances with a fractional distribution over completion times.
release: An α-point selects a position in a fractional schedule. The proof must connect the selected position to an actual feasible schedule and then integrate its cost over the random choice of α.
Routing changes the obstacle from time feasibility to simultaneous congestion on many edges.
flow: Independent path choices have the right expected loads but can overload an edge. Write a tail bound for one normalized edge load, then choose the congestion factor so a union bound controls all edges.
Dense coloring instead samples information about an unknown global partition.
dense-color: A small sample can expose a global partition

The sample is useful because a dense neighborhood is unlikely to be missed. Enumerate its possible colorings, extend the compatible ones, and keep the probability calculation separate from the extension argument.
The next chapter replaces sampled discrete labels with vectors and geometric rounding.
sdp-cut: An angle becomes a separation probability

Represent the relaxation by vectors and choose a random hyperplane. The central calculation takes place in the plane spanned by two endpoint vectors; the guarantee follows from comparing that probability with the SDP contribution.
Vector coloring uses the same geometry but must produce many compatible color classes.
color-sdp: A partial coloring is not a full coloring

Vector constraints produce a rounding procedure that colors a substantial subset. Track the size of that subset and the cost of recursion explicitly before quoting an exponent for a complete coloring.
Gaussian thresholding gives another route from vector separation to large independent sets.
gaussian-color: Marginal survival does not control conflicting pairs
Project vectors onto a Gaussian direction and keep vertices above a threshold. A useful independent set requires both a lower bound on the number kept and an upper bound on surviving edges.
Primal–dual algorithms will produce their guarantees by cost accounting rather than geometric probability.
dual-cover: A feasible dual is a certificate you can spend
Raise uncovered elements until a set becomes tight. A tight set pays for its own cost; the approximation factor comes from the maximum number of selected sets that can charge the same element.
For paths, tightness alone does not prevent redundant selected edges.
dual-path: Selection and cleanup play different roles
The growth phase finds tight edges. Reverse deletion then removes redundant choices. The cost proof must describe the cleaned path, rather than charging every edge ever selected.
The forest lemma extends this kind of charging to many simultaneously growing components.
steiner: Why a forest has enough leaves for charging

Grow active moats, select tight edges, then prune. The approximation factor is a bound on how selected forest edges meet active components; it is not a bound on the degree of each component separately.
Tree metrics simplify a different obstacle: arbitrary geometry.
tree-metrics: A distribution over trees can preserve expected cost

A single dominating tree may distort some pairs badly. Randomization permits an expectation bound for each pair; linearity then transfers the cost of a fixed solution, with algorithmic adaptation checked separately.
Planar layers give another structural reduction, this time to bounded-width pieces.
planar-mis: Delete a little, solve the rest exactly
Delete one residue class of planar layers. One choice loses only a small share of an optimal independent set; bounded treewidth makes the remaining instance tractable by dynamic programming.
The hardness lecture asks which guarantees cannot be achieved without exploiting extra structure.
hardness: A decision reduction needs a quantitative gap
Specify the objective values in YES and NO instances before discussing approximation. A reduction proves hardness only when the proposed ratio forces an algorithm to distinguish those two intervals.
Use this convention check whenever an examiner switches between maximization and minimization.
lfkn-permanent: How can a verifier check a number it cannot compute?

Replace a huge computation by a short sequence of algebraic claims. The prover sends a polynomial before seeing the next random point; a false claim must either be exposed now or survive at a root of a nonzero polynomial.
Next, keep track of which counting problems reduce to this verifier and which closure statements need an additional argument.
lfkn-consequences: A protocol theorem is not yet a hierarchy collapse
Start from the precise counting capability supplied by LFKN. A consequence about oracle computation, program checking, or a hierarchy needs its own reduction and resource accounting.
Shamir extends the algebraic mechanism to quantified formulas, where unbounded degree growth becomes the central obstruction.
qbf: Boolean conjunction and disjunction have simple polynomial versions, but repeated quantifier elimination can double degrees. Multilinearization preserves values on the Boolean cube and creates a low-degree chain the verifier can audit.
The reverse containment evaluates an interaction in polynomial space; private verifier coins require special care.
private-ip: A prover sees a transcript, not the verifier’s random tape

Hidden random tapes that produce the same visible messages must share one prover response. Group those tapes first, then maximize over a legal response. Otherwise the recurrence gives the prover information that the protocol hides.
BFL strengthens the verifier by separating provers rather than increasing its local computation.
bfl-oracle: Isolation turns separate answers into one object
With one prover, answers can adapt to the entire question. A second isolated prover can be asked only for an index; consistency ties the first prover’s answer to a single fixed response function.
That function can still be arbitrary. The next lecture explains what a multilinearity test must establish about it.
bfl-multilinear: Local acceptance must lead to a global polynomial

Passing a few line checks is not the definition of being multilinear. The proof needs a quantitative proximity theorem, followed by self-correction and a consistency argument for the recovered object.
The main NEXP theorem composes these ingredients with an encoding of an exponentially long witness.
bfl-nexp: Audit both sides of the equality

The easy inclusion guesses full prover strategies and evaluates the verifier; the hard inclusion encodes a long computation and checks it locally. Keep the lengths of witnesses, strategies, queries, and random strings explicit.
Zero knowledge asks a different question: can the verifier perform a convincing check while learning nothing extra?
gmw-def: Write the simulator quantifier before the protocol

Completeness and soundness concern whether a claim is accepted. Zero knowledge compares entire verifier views. For each cheating verifier we need a simulator whose output has the required distribution, including its auxiliary input and random tape.
Graph nonisomorphism exposes why an honest-verifier simulation is not the whole malicious-verifier proof.
gmw-gni: A hidden bit gives soundness, but not the whole simulation

Under isomorphism, the two challenge distributions are identical, so an unbounded prover cannot infer the hidden bit better than chance. The complete GMW construction also has to control a malicious verifier’s challenge formation.
Commitments let the NP construction hide a witness while opening just the piece the verifier requests.
gmw-np: Local openings must come from one committed coloring

The prover commits to a randomly relabeled coloring and opens one challenged edge. Binding supplies soundness; hiding supports simulation. Neither property alone proves both claims, and sequential repetition must be analyzed in the same model.
Return to the paper’s exact definitions before extending the protocol to another repetition or commitment model.
four-functions: A statement about four functions contains correlation

Work on the Boolean lattice of subsets. The pointwise hypothesis compares two inputs with their union and intersection; induction converts that local comparison into a statement about four total masses.
FKG chooses the four functions using a measure and increasing events.
fkg: Monotonicity is only half of the hypothesis
Increasing events need not correlate under an arbitrary measure. Check log-supermodularity of the measure, then encode the desired event inequality as an instance of Four Functions.
For product measures the lattice condition is automatic, and a direct inductive proof becomes available.
harris: Condition on one coordinate and track two terms

Conditional correlation handles the remaining coordinates; monotonicity controls the covariance between the two conditional means. The proof explains exactly where independence of the coordinates enters.
The XYZ theorem uses a more structured probability space built from linear extensions.
xyz: Order events live in a dependent sample space
Uniformly random linear extensions are constrained permutations. Translate the events into counts of extensions of related partial orders; the correlation claim requires its order-theoretic argument.
Chapter 7 turns from signs of correlation to quantitative concentration around typical values.
azuma: Choose the exposure before quoting the inequality

Reveal independent data gradually and take conditional expectations of the target variable. A Doob martingale appears automatically; the real work is proving a bounded increment using a coupling of future completions.
Chromatic concentration shows how a careful exposure can beat an edge-by-edge sensitivity estimate.
chromatic: A useful martingale depends on what you expose

A vertex exposure changes many edges but can change chromatic number by at most one after the right comparison. Combine concentration with the structural or packing input needed for the claimed window.
Gradations refine this accounting when queries are adaptive rather than fixed in advance.
gradation: Charge information as it is revealed

Adaptive queries change which random variable is exposed next. Condition on the history and justify every variance or range charge under that conditional law; a deterministic query order cannot simply be assumed.
The applications lecture practices this choice of exposure and sensitivity in several different settings.
azuma-app: The Lipschitz constant is part of the proof
For each target variable, specify a coordinate change, construct the comparison, and count its maximum effect. The same concentration theorem can be strong or useless depending on this modeling step.
Talagrand’s geometry addresses examples where worst-case bounded differences wastes too much information.
talagrand: Distance should remember how a bad event is witnessed

Hamming distance counts changed coordinates equally. Convex distance weights them and measures separation from an event; the product-space inequality turns that geometric separation into a tail estimate.
Certificates connect this distance to concrete witnesses for large values of a random variable.
certificate: A short witness can sharpen a tail bound

A large value may be certified by revealing only a few coordinates. Combine that certificate size with local sensitivity, keeping the distinction between a median-centered statement and a mean-centered one.
Polynomial concentration uses a different summary: expectations of partial derivatives.
kim-vu: A polynomial count such as triangles has overlapping monomials. Inspect expected derivatives at every relevant order to locate the scale of influential coordinates before invoking the concentration theorem.
Chapter 15 uses probability as a construction and strategy tool rather than only a tail estimate.
shannon: Small error is a distributional promise
A finite repetition code makes the error event tangible. For asymptotic random coding, split atypical channel noise from confusion with a second codeword; each event has its own bound.
The Liar Game replaces a stochastic channel by an adaptive adversary, so the counting argument is no longer a complete strategy.
liar: A volume bound can rule out a strategy without constructing one

Count the transcripts compatible with each possible secret, including the lie budget. The total weight yields a necessary capacity bound. A successful adaptive strategy must also split the successor weights at every move.
Tenure uses a weighted potential to expose an exact threshold in a different game.
tenure: Find the invariant behind the threshold
Encode a game position with dyadic weights and check the change under each allowed move. A numerical potential must be paired with a legal response rule to prove the claimed player can win.
Vector balancing replaces discrete levels with coordinates of a running sum.
balancing: The adversary can react to the past
At each round the next vector may depend on previous signs. Condition on the current history before analyzing a randomized sign, and use the potential to control all coordinates simultaneously.
The Half-Liar Game changes which false answers are permitted; the state accounting must change too.
half-liar: One-sided errors have a different state space
An answer consumes a lie allowance only in the permitted direction. Track the clean and already-used states separately; the small k=1 case is a useful place to verify both necessity and strategy.
Entropy provides another way to account for how many possibilities remain.
entropy: An extremal count can be an information calculation
Choose a uniformly random object from a family so its entropy equals the logarithm of the family size. Reveal coordinates with the chain rule and use conditioning carefully to obtain an upper bound.
Shearer’s inequality repeats this idea across overlapping projections, where coordinate multiplicity is decisive.
shearer: Overlapping views must cover every coordinate
Order the coordinates once, expand each projection by the chain rule, and compare conditional entropies term by term. Every coordinate must appear at least the required number of times.
Property testing returns to sampling: a small view must reveal a global obstruction with controlled probability.
tester-color: A sample needs a soundness theorem

A small induced graph that is not 3-colorable is a valid rejection certificate. The difficult direction says that a graph far from the property yields such a sample with noticeable probability; a restriction tree supplies that argument.
Triangle removal gives a particularly clean example of converting structure into a tester.
triangle-removal: Many forbidden copies make a small sample informative

The removal lemma is the structural input: being far from triangle-free forces many triangles. Once that density is available, the algorithmic proof counts the chance of witnessing one and chooses the sample size.
Hereditary properties require induced obstructions and may have infinitely many forbidden graphs.
hereditary: Preservation under induced subgraphs is the key condition

One-sided sampling can reject only through a forbidden induced subgraph. The induced removal theorem supplies a bounded witness size for each distance threshold; its dependence on that threshold is part of the guarantee.
Finish by comparing ordinary removal, induced removal, and the exact sampling model in the assigned chapter.

core-lfkn-permanent.title: Write out the algebraic verification, not just its slogan
core-lfkn-permanent.scope: A sum-check derivation and an explicit inclusion–exclusion presentation of permanent verification. Read the complete LFKN paper for its reductions, protocol organization, and consequences.

steps.title: 1. Define the exact claim
steps.text: Let h be an efficiently evaluable polynomial over a finite field F, with individual degree at most d. The claimed value is its sum on the Boolean cube. The verifier can evaluate h at one field point even though it cannot enumerate the cube.

steps.title: 2. Fix the message before sampling
steps.text: In round i the honest message sums out all still-Boolean variables. The verifier rejects a degree above d or a failure of the two-endpoint identity. Only after receiving this polynomial does it choose a fresh uniform field element.

steps.title: 3. Propagate a false claim
steps.text: If the current claim is false, an accepted message cannot equal the honest polynomial: their endpoint sums differ. Two distinct degree-d polynomials agree at at most d points. Thus a random evaluation repairs the false claim with probability at most d/|F|. Condition on the full past when applying this argument.
steps.tex: C_i=q_i(r_i),\qquad \Pr[\text{a false claim becomes true in round }i\mid\text{past}]\leq d/|F|.

steps.title: 4. Close the chain and count the errors
steps.text: After the last round the verifier evaluates h directly. If the starting claim was false but all tests pass, some round must have changed a false claim into a true one. Union-bound those events. Honest polynomials satisfy every identity, giving perfect completeness.

steps.title: 5. See why permanent admits this type of check
steps.text: Expand the product below. A choice of one column for every row survives the alternating subset sum only if it uses every column, hence is a permutation. On Boolean inputs, each factor 1−2xⱼ supplies the alternating sign. The resulting h is evaluable with polynomially many operations and has individual degree at most n+1. This explicitly demonstrates the algebraic mechanism, rather than replacing the assigned paper’s development.

steps.title: 6. State the arithmetic convention
steps.text: A field computation verifies the permanent modulo that field’s characteristic. An exact integer claim additionally needs a field large enough to prevent wraparound, or a justified reconstruction from residues. The integer permanent of a binary matrix is at most n!, whose bit length is polynomial in n. Message lengths, degree bounds, and field arithmetic must all remain polynomial.

core-lfkn-consequences.title: Move from one algebraic protocol to a class statement
core-lfkn-consequences.scope: The containment chain below identifies the reductions that must be supplied. The complete LFKN paper also treats program checking and relativization.

steps.title: 1. Distinguish function evaluation from a language
steps.text: A claim that a counting function has a stated value is a decision problem for an interactive verifier. A theorem about a polynomial-time oracle computation requires simulation of its adaptively chosen claims, not merely one call.

steps.title: 2. Budget polynomially many oracle checks
steps.text: For q oracle claims, choose each algebraic check’s error at most η/q. Condition on the preceding transcript, identify the first false oracle answer, and apply soundness there. An honest oracle transcript satisfies completeness. This is the resource-and-error accounting needed before invoking the counting reduction.

steps.title: 3. Name the external counting and hierarchy inputs
steps.text: State the relevant completeness reduction to permanent, its arithmetic convention, and the theorem placing the polynomial hierarchy inside polynomial-time counting-oracle computation. These are additional results, not conclusions of the polynomial root bound alone.

steps.title: 4. Keep containment separate from collapse
steps.text: A containment in interactive proofs does not identify the hierarchy with a fixed level. To claim a collapse, specify the extra hypothesis and show how it removes or bounds the alternations. For program checking, likewise define which incorrect function values the checker must detect and what access it has.

core-qbf.title: Track degrees through one quantifier and one reduction
core-qbf.scope: These calculations explain the degree-control mechanism. The complete Shamir protocol fixes the full operator order and bounds every resulting verifier round.

steps.title: 1. Arithmetize Boolean connectives
steps.text: Use variables taking values 0 or 1. The formulas below agree with NOT, AND, and OR on that cube. Quantifier elimination then represents universal quantification by a product and existential quantification by one minus the product of complements.
steps.tex: \neg a\mapsto1-a,\qquad a\wedge b\mapsto ab,\qquad a\vee b\mapsto a+b-ab.

steps.title: 2. Observe the degree problem
steps.text: If the current polynomial has degree d in a remaining variable, multiplying two restrictions can raise that degree to 2d. Repeating this through many quantifiers produces an exponential degree bound unless a reduction is inserted.

steps.title: 3. Reduce one variable without changing Boolean values
steps.text: The selector interpolates between the two Boolean restrictions. At Xⱼ=0 or 1 it returns the corresponding value, and its degree in Xⱼ is at most one. It need not agree with the old polynomial away from the Boolean cube; the protocol must explicitly verify this transformation.

steps.title: 4. Audit a concrete degree reduction
steps.text: For f(X,Y)=X²Y+XY² the reduction in X is XY+XY²; reducing Y next gives 2XY. This agrees with f at all four Boolean points. It does not agree at a general field point: at (2,3), f is 30 and its multilinear reduction is 12. Thus “preserves the polynomial” is a wrong justification.

steps.title: 5. Verify the operator chain backward
steps.text: Arrange a polynomial-length sequence of quantifier and degree-reduction operators. Starting from the claimed truth value, ask for the low-degree univariate restriction needed to undo the next operator, test its defining identity, then replace one coordinate by fresh randomness. The first false-to-true transition is again a root event.

steps.title: 6. Count rounds, degrees, and field bits separately
steps.text: If there are T operator checks with degree bounds D₁,…,Dₜ, soundness is bounded by their sum divided by the field size. In the scheduled construction these parameters are polynomial in the formula length. Choose a sufficiently large field with polynomial bit length and verify that the final arithmetized formula is efficiently evaluable.

core-private-ip.title: Why maximization must stay outside hidden randomness
core-private-ip.scope: A polynomial-space upper-bound argument for a normalized polynomial-message verifier, including private verifier randomness.

steps.title: 1. Fix the visible information
steps.text: Normalize the verifier to a fixed polynomial message schedule, padding halted transcripts. Its random tape has polynomial length. At a prover turn, many random tapes may still be compatible with the same visible transcript; the prover must choose one answer for all of them.

steps.title: 2. Use an information-set recurrence
steps.text: Let S be the compatible tapes, weighted by their prior probability, and let V(r,a) denote the continuation contribution for tape r after a visible prover answer a. The legal maximization has the form below. The alternative permits an answer depending on a tape the prover has not seen.

steps.title: 3. Test the distinction on two hidden tapes
steps.text: Take two equally likely tapes. On the first, answer 0 wins; on the second, answer 1 wins. One legal answer wins with probability 1/2. A separate maximizing answer for each tape wins with probability 1. This is exactly the information leak the recurrence must prevent.

steps.title: 4. Recompute instead of storing the tree
steps.text: At verifier turns, group tapes by the next visible verifier message. Enumerate possible polynomial-length messages and answers one at a time. Membership in a transcript’s compatible-tape set can be recomputed by simulating the verifier. The recursion depth is polynomial; exponential branching increases time, not the stored stack depth.

steps.title: 5. Bound arithmetic space
steps.text: For uniform random tapes of length R, all acceptance probabilities have denominator 2ᴿ. Their numerators require O(R) bits. Store loop indices, transcript prefixes, accumulated numerators, and one recursive branch at a time. This gives polynomial space, with no claim of polynomial running time.

core-bfl-oracle.title: Extract the one object to which consistency refers
core-bfl-oracle.scope: This is the consistency mechanism. BFL’s full oracle characterization also supplies the precise verifier simulation and error parameters.

steps.title: 1. Fix deterministic strategies
steps.text: For a fixed input and fixed shared random seed, each isolated prover’s response is a function of its own question only. Averaging permits fixing a seed when analyzing maximum acceptance, so randomization does not create a new dependence on the other question.

steps.title: 2. Define the oracle before testing a view
steps.text: Let π(i) be the second prover’s answer when asked index i. The first prover supplies a proposed local view on several indices. The verifier selects one of those indices and checks that the view’s entry equals π(i). The second prover must not receive the rest of the view.

steps.title: 3. Quantify one consistency failure
steps.text: If a proposed k-entry view disagrees with π at t entries and the verifier checks a uniformly random entry, it detects disagreement with probability t/k. Small local disagreement and global satisfiability are separate issues; later algebraic tests connect them.

steps.title: 4. Identify the failure under communication
steps.text: If the second prover learns the first prover’s whole question or answer, it can match that particular view without defining a fixed π. State the isolation assumption when moving from a two-prover protocol to an oracle proof.

core-bfl-multilinear.title: Separate the algebra from the testing theorem
core-bfl-multilinear.scope: The extension and exact correction calculation below are elementary. The robust multilinearity/proximity theorem and its composition are substantive inputs proved in the assigned BFL paper.

steps.title: 1. Build the unique extension
steps.text: For a table a on the Boolean cube, the product basis below is 1 at its own Boolean point and 0 at the others. The resulting polynomial agrees with a everywhere on the cube and has individual degree at most one. Induction or the same interpolation basis proves uniqueness.

steps.title: 2. Keep the two line notions distinct
steps.text: A multilinear polynomial restricts to an affine function along a coordinate line. Along a general affine line X=z+tv it can have degree as large as m. A line test or correction procedure must use the bound corresponding to the line it actually samples.

steps.title: 3. State the missing global implication
steps.text: The verifier receives an arbitrary table, not a promise of multilinearity. The required testing theorem says that sufficiently high acceptance implies closeness to one global multilinear polynomial, with quantitative error and field-size conditions. Listing sampled checks is not a proof of that theorem.

steps.title: 4. Explain exact self-correction first
steps.text: If the oracle is exactly a degree-m polynomial, choose a random line through the desired point and interpolate its univariate restriction from m+1 distinct nonzero parameters. Evaluating the interpolant at zero recovers the desired value. The field must provide enough distinct parameters.

steps.title: 5. Then add noise and consistency
steps.text: For an oracle merely close to the polynomial, the correction analysis must bound the probability that queried points are corrupted and handle correlations in the sampling. Compose this with the proximity theorem and two-prover consistency. Name those error terms before adding them; exact interpolation alone does not establish robust decoding.

core-bfl-nexp.title: Account for exponentially long strategies and witnesses
core-bfl-nexp.scope: A proof architecture with the elementary upper bound and explicit lower-bound inputs. The BFL multilinearity and encoding lemmas remain required reading.

steps.title: 1. Prove the upper bound by guessing tables
steps.text: For a verifier using polynomially many random bits and polynomial-length questions and answers, each deterministic prover strategy is a table of at most exponentially many polynomial-length answers. A nondeterministic exponential-time machine can guess the tables.

steps.title: 2. Evaluate all random strings
steps.text: For each verifier random string, simulate its interaction using the guessed local strategies. Count accepting strings and compare with the completeness/soundness threshold using exact integer arithmetic. The total enumeration is exponential, giving MIP ⊆ NEXP.

steps.title: 3. Encode the long witness for the lower bound
steps.text: A NEXP computation has an exponentially long tableau. Encode its local constraints algebraically and access the encoding by short queries. This establishes the object to test; it does not yet prevent inconsistent or non-polynomial responses.

steps.title: 4. Compose three obligations
steps.text: Two-prover consistency supplies a fixed oracle, multilinearity testing supplies proximity to a global polynomial, and algebraic checks verify the encoded computation. If the computation is invalid, at least one obligation must fail with the required probability. The field size, robustness losses, and composition constants must be tracked from the paper.

steps.title: 5. State the model before its consequences
steps.text: The theorem uses classical isolated provers. A consequence about circuits or another prover model needs a separate argument. In particular, a different model of correlations between provers cannot be inserted into the same soundness proof without verification.

core-gmw-def.title: Compare complete views under the right quantifiers
core-gmw-def.scope: A graph-isomorphism honest-verifier simulation illustrates the distribution calculation. It does not replace the paper’s malicious-verifier definitions and transformations.

steps.title: 1. Specify what the verifier receives
steps.text: The view includes the verifier’s auxiliary input, random tape, and messages received, together with any output being compared. State whether equality, statistical distance, or computational indistinguishability is required.

steps.title: 2. Calculate the graph-isomorphism transcript
steps.text: For an honest verifier, sample a uniform challenge b and a uniform relabeling σ of Gᵦ; output the commitment graph H=σ(Gᵦ), challenge b, and opening σ. If G₀ and G₁ are isomorphic, both give the same uniform distribution over labeled copies. This yields the honest transcript law without knowing the witness isomorphism.

steps.title: 3. Check a changed verifier
steps.text: A cheating verifier may choose its challenge as a function of H, its random tape, and auxiliary input. Sampling an independent b no longer matches that interaction. A malicious-verifier simulator needs its own strategy, often involving guessing and rewinding, together with a bound on expected running time.

steps.title: 4. Keep soundness on a separate page
steps.text: For nonisomorphic inputs, a commitment graph cannot be correctly opened as a relabeling of both input graphs. A uniform challenge is answered with probability at most 1/2. This acceptance argument says nothing by itself about what an arbitrary verifier learns.

core-gmw-gni.title: Locate the gap between hidden-bit soundness and simulation
core-gmw-gni.scope: The hidden-bit calculation is a building block. The complete malicious-verifier GMW construction includes challenge certification and its simulator; those cannot be dropped.

steps.title: 1. Define the honest experiment
steps.text: The verifier chooses b uniformly and sends a uniformly relabeled copy of Gᵦ. If the graphs are nonisomorphic, an unbounded prover identifies the isomorphism class and returns b, giving completeness.

steps.title: 2. Prove soundness on isomorphic graphs
steps.text: If G₀ and G₁ are isomorphic, the conditional laws of H given b=0 and b=1 are identical. Therefore b remains uniform after H is revealed, and any prover guesses it with probability at most 1/2.

steps.title: 3. Examine an arbitrary challenge
steps.text: A malicious verifier can send a graph it did not generate by the stated experiment. The honest prover’s response to that graph may encode hard isomorphism information. A simulator for honestly generated challenges is therefore insufficient.

steps.title: 4. Recover the full construction’s obligation
steps.text: The certification phase must constrain challenge formation in a way that lets the simulator obtain the information it needs while preserving completeness and soundness. State the certificate, its extraction or simulation guarantee, and the expected-time analysis from the paper. The bare hidden-bit exchange must not be labeled the full malicious-verifier zero-knowledge proof.

core-gmw-np.title: Audit binding, hiding, and the simulator separately
core-gmw-np.scope: The standard graph-coloring construction explains the NP mechanism. Exact versus negligible soundness depends on the commitment convention, and the GMW paper supplies the full cryptographic and simulation argument.

steps.title: 1. Specify the experiment
steps.text: Randomly permute the three color names and commit to every vertex color. The verifier chooses a uniformly random edge. Open its two endpoint commitments; reject an invalid opening, an invalid color, or equal endpoint colors.

steps.title: 2. Prove completeness
steps.text: A proper coloring gives distinct valid endpoint colors on every edge under every permutation, so every honest commitment and opening is accepted.

steps.title: 3. Derive single-round soundness from binding
steps.text: Under ideal binding, one color is fixed per vertex before the challenge. If every color is valid, a non-3-colorable graph has a monochromatic edge. If some color is invalid, any incident edge fails; isolated vertices can be removed. Thus for a nonempty edge set at least one challenge edge rejects. With computational binding, add the appropriate negligible cheating term.

steps.title: 4. Derive the honest opening distribution
steps.text: For any fixed edge of a proper coloring, a random permutation makes its ordered endpoint colors uniform over the six distinct ordered color pairs. A simulator can produce that local pair without knowing the coloring. Commitments to unopened vertices must still be handled by hiding.

steps.title: 5. Explain guessing and rewinding
steps.text: A simulator can guess an edge to be opened, prepare compatible commitments, and rewind if the verifier asks another edge. Proving success probability and matching the full view against an arbitrary verifier requires the commitment-hiding and hybrid argument. It is not justified by the six-pair calculation alone.

steps.title: 6. Return from coloring to NP
steps.text: Use a polynomial reduction from the original NP statement to 3-colorability and explain how witnesses map forward. The construction’s cryptographic assumption, expected-time simulation model, auxiliary-input convention, and repetition model must remain attached to the theorem.

core-four-functions.title: Prove the two-point lemma, then perform the induction
core-four-functions.scope: A complete finite Boolean-lattice argument. The extension to a finite distributive lattice additionally uses an operation-preserving set representation.

steps.title: 1. Retain all four hypotheses
steps.text: On a one-coordinate lattice write the function values with subscripts 0 and 1. The two cross products have the same union and intersection, so they share one bound C. Nonnegativity is used throughout.

steps.title: 2. Handle the positive denominator
steps.text: If C>0, both γ₁ and δ₀ are positive. The diagonal inequalities give lower bounds on γ₀ and δ₁. Substitute those bounds in the output product and expand. The remainder factors as below, and both factors in its numerator are nonnegative by the cross hypotheses.

steps.title: 3. Do not divide in the zero case
steps.text: If C=0, the cross products are zero. Adding the two diagonal bounds now suffices, since the input product contains only its diagonal terms. The output product contains the diagonal terms plus additional nonnegative terms.

steps.title: 4. Compress one coordinate
steps.text: For each subset A of the first n−1 coordinates, add the two values corresponding to A and A∪{n}. Fix A and B. The four hypotheses for their two lifts have precisely the form of the two-point lemma, with the output lifts indexed by A∪B and A∩B.

steps.title: 5. Invoke induction only after checking its hypothesis
steps.text: The compressed functions are nonnegative and satisfy the same local condition on n−1 coordinates, so induction applies. Each original subset belongs to exactly one pair of lifts, hence each compressed total equals its original total. Substitute all four identities to finish. The zero-coordinate case is the original single point inequality.

core-knapsack.title: Derive the approximation and the running time together
core-knapsack.scope: The basic profit-scaled FPTAS for binary-encoded, nonnegative-profit 0–1 knapsack. Infeasible items are removed before defining the scale.

steps.title: 1. Get a computable lower bound
steps.text: Remove items heavier than the capacity W. If no positive-profit feasible item remains, the empty set is optimal. Otherwise let P be the largest remaining profit. A single best item is feasible, and no solution uses more than n items.

steps.title: 2. Keep exact weights in the dynamic program
steps.text: Let Dᵢ(q) be the minimum original weight of a subset of the first i items with scaled profit q; impossible states have value infinity. Initialize D₀(0)=0. For each item use the better of skipping it and adding its original weight. Return a feasible state with maximum scaled profit. Feasibility is exact because weights were never rounded.

steps.title: 3. Compare to an optimum in the rounded objective
steps.text: For an original optimum O and the returned set S, the DP maximizes scaled profit among all feasible subsets. The floor loses less than K per item, so transferring back to original profits loses at most nK.

steps.title: 4. Count states in terms of input length
steps.text: Every remaining item has profit at most P, so its scaled profit is at most n/ε. The total scaled-profit range is at most n²/ε. The elementary DP therefore has O(n³/ε) transitions. Stored weights are sums of at most n binary inputs and require only polynomially many bits; rational scale arithmetic also uses polynomial bit length.

steps.title: 5. Identify what would break the proof
steps.text: Scaling weights could make a selected set infeasible after restoration. A DP polynomial in the numerical capacity W need not be polynomial in its binary input length. The FPTAS requires polynomial dependence jointly on input size and 1/ε, not merely polynomial time for each fixed ε.

core-azuma.title: Derive the martingale tail from a conditional MGF
core-azuma.scope: Azuma’s inequality under the bounded-increment convention |Mᵢ−Mᵢ₋₁|≤cᵢ. A sharper conditional-range convention has different constants.

steps.title: 1. State the filtration and the increments
steps.text: Let Mᵢ be a martingale adapted to a filtration Fᵢ and set Dᵢ=Mᵢ−Mᵢ₋₁. The martingale property means that each increment has conditional mean zero. The deterministic bounds cᵢ must hold under every relevant revealed history.

steps.title: 2. Prove the one-step exponential bound
steps.text: Convexity bounds the exponential on [−c,c] by the chord through its endpoints. Conditional expectation and the mean-zero property make the two chord weights equal. Finally cosh(u)≤exp(u²/2), which follows term by term from (2k)!≥2ᵏk!. A zero c gives a zero increment directly.

steps.title: 3. Iterate by the tower property
steps.text: The preceding partial sum is measurable with respect to the preceding history. Pull its exponential outside the conditional expectation and apply the one-step bound. Repeating this argument does not assume independent increments.

steps.title: 4. Optimize the exponential Markov bound
steps.text: For t>0, apply Markov’s inequality with λ>0 and minimize the exponent. If the sum of squared bounds is positive, λ=t/Σcᵢ² is optimal. Apply the same argument to −M for a two-sided bound. If every cᵢ is zero, the martingale is constant.

steps.title: 5. Supply the application-specific step
steps.text: For a Doob martingale Mᵢ=E[f(X)|Fᵢ], the theorem is ready only after the increment bound is proved. Couple future completions under two possible newly exposed coordinates and compare the resulting values of f. A bound on changing one raw input is useful only when that coupling respects the conditional model.

core-shannon.title: Turn the random-code calculation into a reliability statement
core-shannon.scope: Achievability for the binary symmetric channel with crossover p<1/2, using a random code ensemble and average message error. Linearity, maximal error, and efficient decoding need the additional steps stated below.

steps.title: 1. Choose a radius with a strict entropy gap
steps.text: For rate R<1−H₂(p), continuity lets us choose δ>0 with p+δ<1/2 and R+H₂(p+δ)<1. The channel makes more than (p+δ)n errors with probability tending to zero; a concentration bound gives exponential decay for fixed δ.

steps.title: 2. Count likely received words
steps.text: For 0≤a≤1/2, the lower-half Hamming ball satisfies the entropy bound. One proof weights the binomial sum by aʲ(1−a)ⁿ⁻ʲ and compares each term for j≤an with aᵃⁿ(1−a)⁽¹⁻ᵃ⁾ⁿ. The total binomial probability is at most one.

steps.title: 3. Condition on the transmitted word and the noise
steps.text: Choose M=⌊2ⁿᴿ⌋ independent uniform codewords and decode to the unique word within radius (p+δ)n, declaring error if there is no unique choice. For a fixed transmitted index and received word, each other random word is uniform and independent of the channel noise. Bound its chance of entering the decoding ball by its volume divided by 2ⁿ.

steps.title: 4. Average and then fix one codebook
steps.text: Decoding can fail because noise leaves the radius or because another codeword enters the ball. Add the two bounds, average over transmitted messages and codebooks, and fix a codebook whose average error is no larger than that average. Both terms tend to zero. This is an existence theorem, without a running-time guarantee for decoding.

steps.title: 5. Keep the stronger versions separate
steps.text: If the fixed code has average error ε, discard the at most half of messages with individual error above 2ε; the remaining code has maximal error at most 2ε and loses at most 1/n in rate. Removing competing words cannot increase the decoding error. A linear code needs a subspace-compatible random construction from the assigned source; independently choosing codewords does not establish linearity.

core-shearer.title: Derive the projection bound one coordinate at a time
core-shearer.scope: Shearer’s entropy inequality for a finite random vector and a family of coordinate sets in which each coordinate appears at least k times, with k≥1.

steps.title: 1. Fix one coordinate order for every projection
steps.text: Expand each projection’s entropy in increasing coordinate order. Its conditional history contains only the earlier coordinates that lie in that projection. Expanding different projections in incompatible orders would obscure the term-by-term comparison.

steps.title: 2. Add the missing conditioning in the correct direction
steps.text: Conditioning cannot increase entropy, so each term above is at least the corresponding term conditioned on all preceding coordinates. This is a lower bound on each projected entropy, not an upper bound.

steps.title: 3. Count every coordinate’s multiplicity
steps.text: Sum over the coordinate sets. Each full-history term occurs at least k times. Conditional entropy is nonnegative, so additional occurrences can be dropped; the chain rule then reconstructs the entropy of the full vector.

steps.title: 4. Apply the bound to a finite family
steps.text: Choose X uniformly from a finite family A. Its entropy is log₂|A|. Each projection has entropy at most the logarithm of its support size, even though the projected distribution need not be uniform. Exponentiating gives the cardinality inequality.

steps.title: 5. Recover Loomis–Whitney and test the hypothesis
steps.text: Take the n projections that omit one coordinate each. Every coordinate occurs n−1 times, yielding the usual exponent. If a coordinate is uncovered, a family can vary freely in that coordinate while all chosen projections stay fixed; this explains why the multiplicity assumption is indispensable.
